sections.content: Until now you've narrated descriptive sentences about a single subject — Hungary. A historical narrative, though, brings in several different subjects one after another: first one people, then another. Each new subject needs its own past-tense verb, and it matters a lot that the verb's number (singular or plural) matches its subject.

items.spanish: A kelták már az ókorban éltek a Kárpát-medencében.
items.english: The Celts already lived in the Carpathian Basin in antiquity.

items.spanish: Egy kelta törzs, az eraviszkuszok, a mai Budapest területén telepedett le.
items.english: One Celtic tribe, the Eravisci, settled in the area of today's Budapest.

items.spanish: Később más népek is megérkeztek, és a kelták fokozatosan beolvadtak közéjük.
items.english: Later other peoples arrived too, and the Celts gradually became absorbed among them.

sections.content: When several subjects appear in one paragraph, Hungarian marks who did what through the verb's singular/plural ending rather than a subject pronoun (*ők*) — so always check that the subject and the verb agree in number. When introducing a new subject, it's better to repeat the noun (*a rómaiak*, *a hunok*) than to use *ők*, so the reader doesn't lose track of who's who.
